import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 695
*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/695](https://www.erdosproblems.com/695)
-/

open Filter Finset Real

namespace Erdos695

/--
Let $q_1 < q_2 < \cdots$ be a sequence of primes such that $q_{i + 1} \equiv 1 \pmod{q_i}$. Is it
true that
$$
\lim_{k \to \infty} q_k^{1/k} = \infty?
$$
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_695 : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∀ {q : ℕ → ℕ},
      StrictMono q →
      (∀ i, (q i).Prime) →
      (∀ i, q (i + 1) % q i = 1) →
      Tendsto (fun k => (q k : ℝ) ^ (1 / k : ℝ)) atTop atTop := by
  sorry

/--
Is there a sequence of primes $q_1 < q_2 < \cdots$ such that $q_{i + 1} \equiv 1 \pmod{q_i}$ and
$$
q(k) \leq \exp(k (\log k)^{1 + o(1)})?
$$
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_695.variants.upperBound : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∃ q : ℕ → ℕ,
      StrictMono q ∧
      (∀ i, (q i).Prime) ∧
      (∀ i, q (i + 1) % q i = 1) ∧
      ∃ o : ℕ → ℝ,
        (o =o[atTop] (1 : ℕ → ℝ)) ∧
        -- We use `(k + 1)` here as the informal statement is 1-indexed.
        ∀ k, q k ≤ exp ((k + 1) * log (k + 1) ^ (1 + o k)) := by
  sorry

end Erdos695

reformulations.difference: The sequence is zero-indexed, but the exponent is 1/k rather than 1/(k+1). The k = 0 term also uses Lean's division-by-zero convention.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Reindex the source sequence by q(k) = p_{k+1}. Its limit then concerns B_k = q(k)^(1/(k+1)), whereas Lean concerns A_k = q(k)^(1/k). For k ≥ 1 and q(k) ≥ 1, A_k^(1/2) ≤ B_k ≤ A_k. Consequently A_k tends to +∞ exactly when B_k does. The k = 0 term equals 1 and cannot affect the limit. The equivalence between the complete universally quantified right-hand sides was proved as Review695.main_rhs_iff_one_indexed.

reformulations.difference: The source gives an asymptotic upper bound, while Lean requires the displayed inequality at every index. In particular, the bound at k = 0 forces q(0) = 2 and o(0) = -1.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: This does not change the existential question. Given any admissible chain with an eventual bound, replace only its first term by 2. Its second term is an odd prime greater than 2, so strict increase and every congruence are preserved. Set the initial error value to -1; the initial upper bound becomes exp(1) > 2. At every k ≥ 1, log(k+1) is positive and different from 1, so varying the real exponent can make the bound accommodate any fixed prime. Thus all remaining finitely many exceptions can be repaired by changing finitely many error values, preserving o(k) → 0. The reverse implication is immediate. The equivalence for the exact Lean right-hand side was proved as Review695.upper_rhs_iff_eventual.
